children.name: li
children: Protects the provider's internal network and cloud metadata services from user-supplied URLs

children.name: li
children: Contains slow or malicious endpoints so they can't exhaust delivery workers

children.name: li
children: Validating the URL at registration is not enough — DNS and redirects can change where a request goes

children.name: li
children: Requires network-level controls, not just application code

content.name: p
children: Most webhook security focuses on the consumer: is this request really from the provider? But a webhook is an HTTP request the provider makes to a URL chosen by someone else. Malicious users can register webhook URLs that point back into the provider's own network, then use the webhook system to probe internal services — a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attack. Others register endpoints that respond slowly or never respond, tying up delivery workers.

content.name: p
children: summarized the problem well from running a monitoring service that calls user-defined webhooks:

children.name: li
children: Timeouts: the user can set up a webhook receiver that takes very long to generate a response. Your service must be able to deal with that.

children.name: li
children: Timeouts (slowloris): the webhook target could be sending back one byte at a time, with 1 second pauses inbetween. If you are using, say, the "requests" python library for making HTTP requests, the "timeout" parameter will not help here

children.name: li
children: Private IPs and reserved IPs: you probably don't want users defining webhooks to http://127.0.0.1:<some-port> and probing your internal network. Remember about private IPv6 ranges too

children.name: li
children: Domains that resolve to private IPs: attacker could set up foo.com which resolves to a private IP. It is not enough to just validate webhook URLs when users set them up.

children.name: li
children: HTTP redirects to private IPs. If your HTTP client library follows HTTP redirects, the attacker can set up a webhook endpoint that redirects to a private IP. Again, it is not enough to validate the user-supplied URL.

children.name: li
children: Excessive HTTP redirects. The attacker can set up a redirect loop - make sure this does not circumvent your timeout setting.

children.name: li
children: expose instance credentials on most cloud providers. They are the most valuable SSRF target and must be blocked explicitly.

children.name: li
children: delivery logs that show the endpoint's full response body turn a blind SSRF into one that leaks data. Truncate or omit response bodies from requests to unexpected destinations.

content.name: p

children.name: strong
children: Route webhook traffic through an egress proxy.
resolves the destination, blocks private, loopback, link-local, and reserved ranges (IPv4 and IPv6), and is the only path to the internet for delivery workers. The

content.name: p
children: Run them in a network segment with no access to internal services, so a bypass of the proxy still reaches nothing of value. Standard Webhooks recommends a private subnet that can only reach the internet through the proxy.

content.name: p

children.name: strong
children: Check the IP you actually connect to.

Validate the resolved address at send time, then connect to that address — not to the hostname again. Re-resolving lets an attacker return a public IP for the check and a private one for the connection (DNS rebinding).

content.name: p
children: Set a timeout on the whole request, including connecting, TLS, and reading the response, and cap the response size. A per-read timeout doesn't stop a slowloris response.

children: Confirm the endpoint wants your traffic.
proves the URL is controlled by someone expecting webhooks, which prevents a provider from being used to send traffic to arbitrary third-party servers.

frontmatter.title: SSRF and Egress Security
frontmatter.description: When users can register any URL as a webhook endpoint, providers must protect their own infrastructure from Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), slow responses, and redirect tricks.
